Human harms

24 HRM records
HRM-AUT-01Manipulation
A person or accountable principal is steered toward an outcome through materially misleading, asymmetric or exploitative influence.
Autonomy
HRM-AUT-02Coercion
A person faces material penalty, loss or threat unless they accept a system action, disclosure or decision.
Autonomy
HRM-AUT-03Loss of meaningful choice
Nominal consent or choice exists but practical alternatives, information or timing are insufficient for meaningful agency.
Autonomy
HRM-AUT-04Delegation beyond informed intent
A delegated actor performs or enables an action outside the principal’s reasonably understood mandate.
Autonomy
HRM-AUT-05Inability to withdraw or revoke
A person cannot effectively terminate consent, delegated authority, participation or continued processing.
Autonomy
HRM-ACC-01Wrongful exclusion
A legitimate person or organization is denied access, participation or recognition without a justified basis.
Access and inclusion
HRM-ACC-02Discriminatory burden
A rule or system imposes materially higher burdens on a protected, marginalized or structurally disadvantaged group.
Access and inclusion
HRM-ACC-03Accessibility failure
A legitimate participant cannot complete a required interaction because accessibility needs are not supported.
Access and inclusion
HRM-ACC-04Infrastructure dependency exclusion
Access depends on devices, networks, identity infrastructure or services unavailable to some legitimate participants.
Access and inclusion
HRM-PRV-01Unnecessary disclosure
Information beyond the minimum necessary is exposed to a party or system.
Privacy
HRM-PRV-02Linkability and correlation
Separate interactions can be linked to construct a broader profile of a person, organization or agent.
Privacy
HRM-PRV-03Inference beyond disclosed facts
Observed data or metadata enables sensitive conclusions not intentionally disclosed.
Privacy
HRM-PRV-04Persistent surveillance
System operation enables durable observation or reconstruction of activities across time or contexts.
Privacy
HRM-PRV-05Secondary use and context collapse
Information collected for one purpose or audience is reused in another materially different context.
Privacy
HRM-ECO-01Loss of economic opportunity
A system decision prevents or materially reduces access to employment, trade, finance or other economic participation.
Economic
HRM-ECO-02Fraudulent or misallocated liability
A person or organization bears financial or legal consequences for an action they did not authorize or control.
Economic
HRM-GOV-01Arbitrary decision
A consequential decision is taken without consistent rules, sufficient reasons or accountable authority.
Governance and due process
HRM-GOV-02Unavailable appeal or remedy
An affected party lacks a practical path to contest, correct or obtain remedy for an adverse outcome.
Governance and due process
HRM-GOV-03Unaccountable or captured authority
Decision power is exercised without effective oversight, contestability or independence.
Governance and due process
HRM-SEC-01Impersonation and false attribution
Actions or claims are attributed to the wrong person, organization or agent.
Security-mediated harm
HRM-SEC-02Unauthorized consequential action
A system performs a consequential action without current, sufficient authority from the accountable principal.
Security-mediated harm
HRM-SEC-03Denial or disruption of participation
Security or operational failure prevents legitimate use, continuity, recovery or participation.
Security-mediated harm
HRM-INF-01False provenance or trust inference
A party correctly observes an artefact or signature but infers legitimacy, endorsement, authority or quality that it does not establish.
Information integrity
HRM-SAF-01Physical or safeguarding exposure
Digital information or system action materially increases risk of physical harm, stalking, abuse or safeguarding failure.

Glossary

RAHP terms explained in simple English, with stable structured source records for tooling and documentation.

generated by tools/build.py from data/ · 48 risk · 73 control · 25 guardrail · 25 assurance_test · 40 metric · 36 user_story · 33 scenario · 21 epic · 22 persona · 9 recommendation · 3 risk_acceptance · 3 governance_precedent · 1 rule_profile · 5 evidence_artifact

RAHP glossary. These terms use simple English. Structured YAML under method/glossary/terms/ is authoritative.
Agentrahp-native
A software or human actor that takes actions for itself or for another principal.
Example: A software agent requests a credential presentation on behalf of its user.
Applicabilityrahp-native
The conditions under which a risk, control, guardrail or test is relevant.
Example: A cross-context privacy guardrail applies only when correlation is not necessary for the declared purpose.
Assurancerahp-native
Reasoned confidence, supported by evidence, that a system or control behaves as claimed.
Example: A replay test and its retained trace support confidence that duplicate execution is blocked.
AT-*ATP-*
Assurance levelrahp-native
A label for how strong the assurance evidence is, from basic inspection to stronger independent or automated evidence.
Example: A2 may require repeatable tests while A0 may only record that no assurance has been shown.
A0A1A2A3A4
Assurance patternrahp-native
A reusable testable claim about a control or guardrail, including how to test it and what evidence to keep.
Example: Try a revoked delegation and confirm the action is blocked.
ATP-*
Audiencerahp-native
The party or set of parties for whom a message, credential, proof or authority grant is intended.
Example: A proof created for one verifier should not automatically be reused by another.
Audit eventrahp-native
A recorded event that shows a control, guardrail, decision or override was evaluated or used.
Example: The log records that authority was checked and that an override was rejected.
Auditabilityrahp-native
The ability to reconstruct what happened, which rules were used, who acted and what evidence supported the result.
Example: An investigator can trace a delegated action back to the principal and active mandate.
Authenticationrahp-native
A process that establishes which actor, account, key or system is presenting itself.
Example: A signature verifies that a message came from a known key.
Authorityrahp-native
The legitimate power to make a decision, request an action or change governed state.
Example: A valid signature proves who signed; it does not by itself prove that the signer had authority to approve payment.
Authorizationrahp-native
A decision about whether an actor is allowed to perform a particular action in a particular context.
Example: An authenticated agent may still be denied permission to transfer funds.
Composition boundaryrahp-native
The point where one specification, protocol or system relies on facts produced by another.
Example: A task engine accepts a credential status result from a separate credential system.
Consequential actionrahp-native
An action that can materially affect rights, money, access, safety, authority, privacy or an external system state.
Example: Revoking access, transferring money or publishing a credential are consequential actions.
Contestabilityrahp-native
The ability to understand, challenge and seek correction or remedy for a consequential outcome.
Example: A person can see why access was denied and submit evidence for review.
Context bindingrahp-native
A rule that ties evidence, authority or a credential to the task, transaction, audience or purpose where it is meant to be used.
Example: A witness credential names the trust task that produced it.
Controlrahp-native
A deployment-specific measure used to reduce, detect, contain or recover from a risk.
Example: A verifier checks status immediately before approving a transaction.
CT-*
Control patternrahp-native
A reusable control objective that deployments can apply in their own way.
Example: Check current authority at the action boundary.
CTP-*
Control side effectrahp-native
A new risk or harm introduced or made worse by a control that was meant to reduce another risk.
Example: Extra identity checks reduce fraud but may increase exclusion or surveillance.
CTP-RISK-01
Cross-spec compositionrahp-native
The combined behavior that appears when two or more specifications or protocols are used together.
Example: A credential can be valid under one specification but stale under the lifecycle rules of another.
RKP-COMP-*
Decision boundaryrahp-native
The point where a system changes from gathering information to making or executing a consequential decision.
Example: The final approval step before an account is disabled is a decision boundary.
Delegationrahp-native
A grant of bounded authority from one actor to another.
Example: A person allows an agent to book one hotel within a price limit.
Enforcement pointrahp-native
The place in a system where a control or guardrail is actually checked and can stop, change or allow an action.
Example: A verifier checks current authorization just before it calls the payment API.
Evidencerahp-native
Information kept to support or challenge an assurance claim, decision or finding.
Example: A signed authorization decision record shows what policy and authority were used.
EV-*EVP-*
Evidence patternrahp-native
A reusable description of what evidence should be produced, who produces it, how fresh it must be and when it becomes invalid.
Example: A revocation propagation trace records when each enforcement point learned about a revocation.
EVP-*
Fail closedrahp-native
To stop or refuse a consequential action when a required safety or assurance condition cannot be established.
Example: If current revocation status cannot be checked, the verifier defers the high-impact action.
Fail openrahp-native
To continue an action even though a check or dependency failed. This must be explicit when it can create risk.
Example: A low-impact read may use a short cached value during a network outage.
Findingrahp-native
A specific observation from a pressure test or security review that needs attention or a recorded disposition.
Example: The specification does not say how a user can challenge an adverse decision.
Finding dispositionrahp-native
The recorded outcome for an earlier finding, such as unchanged, weakened, resolved or superseded.
Example: A new normative replay rule changes a replay finding from open to resolved.
Freshnessrahp-native
How recent information or evidence must be for a decision to rely on it.
Example: A high-impact action may require status checked within the last minute.
Guardrailrahp-native
A rule that blocks or stops an unacceptable state. It is stronger than normal guidance.
Example: Do not let a consequential action proceed when current authority cannot be established.
GR-*GRP-*
Guardrail patternrahp-native
A reusable guardrail that describes what must not be allowed, where it is enforced and what happens on failure.
Example: Do not treat a valid credential as permission for an unrelated action.
GRP-*
Guardrail requirementrahp-native
The catalogue decision that says whether a risk needs a guardrail, needs one only in some conditions, or is adequately handled by controls.
Example: A privacy risk may need a guardrail only when cross-context correlation is not necessary.
RKP-*
Harmrahp-native
A bad effect on a person, group, organization or public interest.
Example: A person is wrongly locked out of an essential service.
HRM-*
Harm patternrahp-native
A reusable description of a kind of harm that can appear in many systems.
Example: Wrongful exclusion can happen in identity, payment or registry systems.
HRM-*
Lifecyclerahp-native
The states an artefact, authority or policy moves through from creation to retirement or invalidation.
Example: A credential can be issued, active, suspended, revoked and expired.
Mandaterahp-native
The purpose and limits under which an actor or agent is expected to act for a principal.
Example: An agent may compare travel options but may not buy one without approval.
Overriderahp-native
A governed exception that allows a normal control or guardrail outcome to be changed by an authorized actor.
Example: An emergency override may be allowed only to a named governance role and must be logged.
Override authorityrahp-native
The role or actor that is allowed to approve an override.
Example: Only the incident commander may approve an emergency continuity override.
Principalrahp-native
The person or organization whose authority, interests or instructions an agent or delegate is expected to serve.
Example: A traveller is the principal when a personal agent books on the traveller’s behalf.
Prohibited staterahp-native
A system state that a guardrail says must not be entered or continued.
Example: A payment proceeds even though required authority cannot be established.
Protected interestrahp-native
The person, group or institutional interest that a guardrail is meant to protect.
Example: Privacy is the protected interest behind a guardrail against unnecessary disclosure.
Provenancerahp-native
Information about where an artefact, action, decision or claim came from and how it changed over time.
Example: A delegation trace shows which principal granted which delegate which scope.
Purposerahp-native
The stated reason for collecting information, making a decision or performing an action.
Example: A credential is requested to confirm age, not to build a marketing profile.
Reassessmentrahp-native
A new review performed because the target, evidence, threat model or operating context has changed.
Example: A specification changes its revocation rules, so earlier findings are checked again.
Recommendationrahp-native
A proposed action to reduce a finding or risk.
Example: Require a fresh authority check immediately before a destructive action.
REC-*
Redressrahp-native
A process that can correct, compensate for or otherwise remedy a harmful or incorrect outcome.
Example: A wrongly excluded user can appeal and have access restored.
Remedyrahp-native
The action taken to correct or reduce the effect of a harmful or incorrect outcome.
Example: A registry corrects an entry and notifies affected relying parties.
Residual riskrahp-native
The risk that remains after controls and guardrails are applied.
Example: A cached status check lowers outage risk but still leaves a short stale-state window.
Retest conditionrahp-native
A stated event that should cause an earlier assurance result or finding to be checked again.
Example: Retest when the specification changes its authorization model.
Revocationrahp-native
A governed act that ends previously granted authority, status or validity.
Example: A principal revokes an agent’s authority to make purchases.
Riskrahp-native
A possible way a specific deployment can cause harm or fail to meet its goals.
Example: A registry may keep an old key after it should have been removed.
RK-*
Risk acceptancerahp-native
A governed decision to live with a known residual risk for a stated period and reason.
Example: A deployment accepts a low-impact availability risk until a replacement service is ready.
RA-*
Risk patternrahp-native
A reusable failure mechanism that can appear in more than one deployment or specification.
Example: A system may mistake proof of identity for permission to act.
RKP-*
Scoperahp-native
The boundary of what an authority, control, assessment or claim applies to.
Example: A delegation may allow read access to one record for one hour.
Stale staterahp-native
Old information that no longer reflects the current authority, status, policy or system condition.
Example: A cached registry entry still points to a key that has been revoked.
Suspensionrahp-native
A governed temporary stop that may later be lifted without creating a new grant from scratch.
Example: A credential is suspended during an investigation and later restored.

RK-SC03

VRC Over-Disclosure — Rich Data in Core Edge

SchemasMediumMediumAll phases
The VRC schema (spec §5.2) requires only the target DID and proof, but places no constraint on what additional data may be embedded in `credentialSubject`. Implementers who embed rich relationship metadata — relationship duration, first-meeting location, mutual endorsements — directly in VRCs rather than using the annotation credential layer (VPC, VEC, VWC) create credentials in which both parties have cryptographically committed to that data. It cannot then be selectively disclosed or withheld from verifiers. The annotation credential architecture exists in the spec but is not normatively required as the channel for supplementary data. **Introduced by:** DTG Credential Spec v0.3 analysis (RAHP commentary §2.4).
Related RAHP artefacts

RK-SC04

M-DID Bootstrapping Exception Undermines R-DID Privacy

SchemasMediumHighPhase 1–3
Spec §5.2 permits M-DIDs 'for bootstrapping' with no normative migration trigger or timeline. The Privacy Considerations section (§9) recommends migration to R-DIDs post-bootstrapping but does not make this a normative requirement. In practice, if migration never happens — the likely outcome without a phase-gate — early VRC relationships remain M-DID-based. An adversary monitoring the trust registry during the bootstrapping phase can reconstruct membership graphs from M-DID co-occurrences in VRCs issued before migration. **Introduced by:** DTG Credential Spec v0.3 §5.2 and Privacy Considerations §9 (RAHP commentary §2.5).
Related RAHP artefacts

RK-CR04

Endorsement Credential (VEC) Manipulation

CredentialsMediumMediumPhase 3–4 / Ongoing
Spec §7.2 defines the VEC's `endorsement` field as 'community/VTN-defined — structure and fields determined by community policy.' This maximum flexibility, with no normative constraint requiring endorsers to be co-members of the same VTC as the endorsed party, creates a reputation manipulation attack surface. A coordinated bad-faith actor can issue large volumes of fabricated VECs with high `competencyLevel` claims to inflate the reputation of synthetic personas, then use those reputational signals to gain governance influence. **Introduced by:** DTG Credential Spec v0.3 §7.2 (RAHP commentary §2.8).

RK-G05

Governanceless VTC Claiming Credential Compliance

GovernanceMediumHighPhase 1
The DTG Credential Specification v0.3 defines credential schemas (§2–§8) and normative credential requirements without requiring that a VTC deploying these credentials has any governance framework in place. A developer group could deploy technically compliant VMCs and VRCs — passing all credential-layer verification checks — while operating with no genesis policy, no time-bounded initiator authority, and no trust anchor diversity requirements. Relying parties would have no normative signal that governance is absent. **Introduced by:** DTG Credential Spec v0.3 analysis — gap identified in §9 (Trust Registries section) and commentary §2.9.

RK-HX04

Incapacity / Unsupported Decision-Making Exclusion

Human ExperienceHighHighPhase 3–4 / Ongoing
The VTC admission and ongoing participation architecture assumes all members are adults with full independent legal capacity. Persons who require supported decision-making — including minors with SEN (EC1), adults with progressive cognitive impairment (EC2a), and others acting under delegated authority — are structurally excluded or forced into non-compliant workarounds. The credential architecture has no concept of co-signed or supported consent distinct from substituted decision-making.

RK-HX05

Legal Capacity Architecture Gap — LPA / Guardianship Not Representable

Human ExperienceHighMediumPhase 3–4 / Revocation / Ongoing
A registered Lasting Power of Attorney (or equivalent legal guardianship instrument) has no representation in the DTG credential architecture. The VTC system cannot distinguish a legitimate LPA holder authenticating on behalf of a donor from an account takeover. Governance communications (revocation notices, renewal reminders, appeals deadlines) are addressed to the credential holder's contact details — which an incapacitated person cannot access — with no secondary recipient mechanism. The LPA holder has no audit-trail separate from the donor, and no defined pathway to close an M-DID on the donor's death.
Related RAHP artefacts
GR-08GR-19CT-59CT-60AT-08AT-19M-02M-07M-26M-30M-33US-29US-30US-31US-32SC-28SC-29
RK-HX06

Credential Lifecycle Abandonment on Capacity Loss or Death

Human ExperienceMediumHighRevocation / Ongoing
When a member loses capacity progressively (e.g., dementia) or dies, the DTG architecture has no defined lifecycle event for credential closure, dormancy, or attorney-mediated continuation. The M-DID simply goes silent. There is no mechanism for the trust graph to record a capacity transition, for credentials to enter an attorney-managed state, or for a death notification to propagate to relying parties. The spec addresses revocation but not the end of life as a credential lifecycle event.
Related RAHP artefacts

RK-ID06

Minor Data Exposure via Co-Signatory Inference

IdentityHighHighPhase 3–4
When a minor (or person lacking full independent capacity) applies to join a VTC, any co-signatory structure in the admission credential implicitly signals that the credential holder has reduced or delegated capacity. This disclosure is not consented to: the minor's SEN status, age, or disability is inferred from the governance structure itself, even if no explicit SEN attribute is included in the credential. The UK Online Safety Act 2023 and the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 impose additional obligations on systems processing children's data, which a VTC admitting under-18s becomes subject to — often without realising it.

RK-EX04

Child Safety Non-Compliance — Age Assurance Failure

ExternalCriticalMediumPhase 4 / Age-Restricted Use Cases
A minor successfully obtains or presents a valid-appearing over-18 IDVC, whether through IDVP failure, synthetic credential generation by Phantom (M2) or Viktor (B1), a ZKP implementation gap (RK-CY01), or an architecture flaw in the age assurance pathway. This is a non-negotiable child safety failure with criminal liability implications under the Online Safety Act 2023 for any age-restricted relying party (e.g., EC4 Velvet Gate). Unlike other register risks, this risk has a binary outcome: any non-zero incident rate is a system-level failure. The Ofcom regime provides no safe harbour for technical failure where the architecture was knowingly immature.
Related RAHP artefacts

RK-EX05

Organisational Identity Architecture Gap

ExternalHighHighPhase 1–4 / Ongoing
The DTG Credential Specification v0.3 defines credential schemas for individual natural persons. An NHS Foundation Trust (EC3) or other regulated organisation seeking to participate as a VTC member holds institutional identity, makes decisions through board governance rather than individual consent, and has complex internal authority chains (Caldicott Guardian, CDO, board resolution) that cannot be represented in the current C-DID model. Regulatory compliance (NHS DSPT, DCB3051, CQC) requires the organisation's governance to be traceable to its credential operations in ways the current architecture does not support. The DTG spec has no organisational credential type.
Related RAHP artefacts
GR-21CT-63CT-64AT-21M-04M-10M-34M-35US-33US-34SC-30SC-31
RK-EX06

IDVP Regulatory Cascade — Cross-Jurisdiction Age Assurance

ExternalHighMediumPhase 4 / Age-Restricted Use Cases
An age-restricted relying party (EC4) relies on IDVCs issued by IDVPs registered in the VTC trust registry. Where subscribers are located internationally, their IDVCs may have been issued by IDVPs whose trust registry standing is uncertain, whose jurisdiction's age verification standards differ from UK Ofcom requirements, or who have subsequently been deregistered or compromised (cf. RK-ID03, AU10TIX breach 2024). The relying party cannot independently verify the current standing of a foreign IDVP in near-real-time without a cross-jurisdiction trust registry resolution mechanism. The Online Safety Act 2023 does not provide a safe harbour for good-faith reliance on a deregistered IDVP.
Related RAHP artefacts
GR-05GR-20CT-13CT-62CT-65AT-05AT-20M-04M-17M-34M-36US-35SC-32
RK-SC05

Credential Schema Gap — Supported Consent and LPA Not Representable

SchemasHighHighPhase 3–4 / Ongoing
The current VRC, VMC, and IDVC schemas assume a single credential holder who is the same legal person as the consent-giver, the DID controller, and the community participant. The schemas have no field or structure for: (a) co-signed admission where the signatory is not a substituted decision-maker; (b) a delegation credential representing a registered LPA; (c) a capacity-status flag indicating that the holder currently operates under supported or substituted decision-making; or (d) a secondary notification recipient registered in the trust registry. These gaps mean the architecture literally cannot represent legal relationships that exist in the real world for an estimated 1.3 million people in England and Wales alone (LPA registrations as of 2025).

VRC Data Minimisation Clause

unassigned
The VRC `credentialSubject` SHOULD contain only the minimum claims necessary for graph structure: the target party's DID and the `validFrom` timestamp. Implementations MUST NOT require VRC subjects to include personal data beyond that strictly required by VTC admission policy. **Source:** DTG Credential Spec v0.3 commentary recommendation R6 (§2.4).

unassigned

The trigger SHOULD occur before Phase 4 opens or before the VTC exceeds a governance-defined membership threshold. After the trigger, new VRCs MUST use R-DIDs. The migration trigger condition and date MUST be recorded in the trust registry. **Source:** DTG Credential Spec v0.3 §5.2 Privacy Considerations and commentary recommendation R7 (§2.5).

RK-HX01RK-ID05RK-SC04GR-18

Non-Human DID Designation in DID Document

unassigned
Agent DIDs MUST be designated as non-human in the DID Document using a defined service type property or a `@type` assertion, enabling VTAs to apply agent-specific policy. VTAs MAY reject VMC applications from DIDs not carrying a human attestation where VTC policy requires proof of personhood. This creates a normative distinction between Aether (M1) and Phantom (M2) at the DID layer. **Source:** DTG Credential Spec v0.3 analysis — gap in §5.1/§5.2 (commentary §2.3, recommendation R1, §10.1).

RK-AI01RK-AI03GR-12

unassigned
An AI agent operating on behalf of a human VTC member MUST hold a delegation credential issued by that member's M-DID, referencing the member's VMC and specifying the agent's permitted capability scope as a normative `credentialSubject` claim. Without this, the spec's VMC schema cannot distinguish an authorised agent (Aether, M1) from an adversarial one (Phantom, M2). **Source:** DTG Credential Spec v0.3 analysis — gap in §5.1 (commentary §2.3, recommendation R1, §10.2).

RK-AI01RK-AI02GR-12

VIC Role Embedding (membershipRole field)

unassigned
The VIC `credentialSubject` SHOULD include a `membershipRole` field specifying the role to be granted upon admission (e.g. 'trustAnchor', 'member'). This allows the issuer to cryptographically commit to the intended role at invitation time, enabling offline verification and making the VIC tamper-evident with respect to role assignment — independent of trust registry availability. The spec's open question ('Q: Should any of this be embedded in the VIC?') in §6.1 should be resolved in this direction. **Source:** DTG Credential Spec v0.3 §6.1 open question (commentary recommendation R4, §2.6).

RK-G01RK-SC02GR-01

unassigned

This directly implements CT-36 (Out-of-Band Verification) using the VWC schema and raises the cost of AI-generated synthetic anchor persona attacks (RK-AI04). The VWC `witnessContext.method` field should record the verification method. **Source:** DTG Credential Spec v0.3 §7.3 (commentary §1.4, recommendation R9).
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-AI04RK-ID01GR-14

unassigned
VTC implementations SHOULD require that Endorsement Credential (VEC per spec §7.2) issuers hold a valid VMC from the same C-DID as the endorsed party. VTA policy enforcement points SHOULD verify this co-membership before treating VEC-based reputation signals as valid inputs to admission or governance decisions. Aggregated VEC metrics SHOULD be treated with appropriate scepticism where endorsements form tight clusters from a small issuer group. **Source:** DTG Credential Spec v0.3 §7.2 — underspecification identified in commentary §2.8, recommendation R10.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-CR04RK-SY02GR-03

At minimum this must include: a genesis policy record (GR-01), a time-bounded initiator authority mechanism (GR-02), and a trust anchor diversity policy (GR-03). The trust registry entry for a DTG-compliant VTC SHOULD include a resolvable reference to its published governance framework. Without this, technical credential compliance provides false assurance to relying parties. **Source:** DTG Credential Spec v0.3 §9 (Trust Registries) — gap identified in commentary §2.9, recommendation R8.

unassigned
Extend the VRC and VMC schema with an optional co-signatory field that distinguishes supported consent (co-signatory assists but member retains decision authority) from substituted consent (attorney acts in place of member). The LDC must: name the attorney and donor DIDs; reference the legal instrument by registration number; constrain the attorney's authorised operations; and be registered in the VTC trust registry as a discoverable relationship distinct from ordinary member credentials.

Secondary Notification Recipient Registration

unassigned
The VTC trust registry and governance communication systems must support registration of one or more secondary notification recipients for a member's credential lifecycle events (revocation notices, renewal reminders, appeals deadlines). Where an LDC is registered, the attorney named in the LDC must be automatically enrolled as a secondary recipient. Secondary recipient communications must be cryptographically authenticated and separate from the primary member account.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-CR01RK-HX05RK-HX06RK-SC05GR-08GR-19
CT-61

M-DID Closure and Death Notification Pathway

unassigned
Define a governed lifecycle pathway for M-DID closure upon death or permanent incapacity, including: a notification mechanism for the trust graph; a tamper-evident closure record; a portability package for the credential history; and an attorney or next-of-kin confirmation workflow. The VTC governing body must publish its M-DID closure procedure as part of its governance documentation.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-HX06RK-SC05GR-08
CT-62

Age Assurance Compliance Verification Requirement

unassigned
Any VTC that admits an age-restricted relying party (i.e., a VTC member or relying party operating under the Online Safety Act 2023 Part 5 or equivalent) must verify that: (a) the ZKP implementation used for age proofs has been independently audited; (b) the IDVP trust registry entry includes an age-verification scope claim; and (c) the relying party's Ofcom-compliant audit record template is reviewed by the VTC governing body before the relying party is admitted. The governing body must maintain documented evidence of this review.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-EX04RK-EX06GR-20
CT-63

Organisational Credential Type Definition

unassigned
Define a new credential type — the Organisational Member Credential (OMC) — that represents an organisation (rather than a natural person) as a VTC participant. The OMC must: identify the organisation by legal identifier (company number, charity number, NHS ODS code, etc.); name the individual officers responsible for credential operations (with their personal DIDs); specify the internal governance process by which the organisation authorises credential actions; and bind the organisation's regulatory compliance status as an attestable claim.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-EX05GR-21
CT-64

Organisational Governance Conformance Mapping

unassigned
For organisations seeking VTC membership, the VTC governing body must assess whether the organisation's existing internal governance framework (e.g., NHS DSPT, CQC registration, ISO 27001) satisfies the VTC governance conformance class (CT-56). Where it does, this equivalence must be formally documented and recorded in the trust registry as an attestable claim, avoiding duplication of governance processes that would be incompatible with public sector procurement timescales.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-EX05GR-21
CT-65

Cross-Jurisdiction IDVP Standing Verification

unassigned
The VTC trust registry must expose a machine-readable, near-real-time IDVP standing endpoint that age-restricted relying parties can query at the point of credential presentation. For IDVPs operating under non-UK regulatory frameworks, the registry must include a jurisdictional scope claim and a date-of-last-verification. Relying parties must not accept IDVCs from IDVPs whose registry standing cannot be confirmed at presentation time for age-assurance use cases.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-EX06RK-ID03GR-05GR-20
CT-66

Children's Data Processing Impact Assessment Requirement

unassigned
Any VTC that knowingly or foreseeably admits participants under the age of 18 (including via supported decision-making pathways for minors) must complete a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) addressing children's data processing obligations under UK GDPR Article 35, the ICO Children's Code, and the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. The DPIA must be completed before the first minor is admitted and reviewed annually. The VTC governing body must designate a named responsible officer for children's data compliance.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-EX03RK-ID06RK-SC05GR-06GR-19
CT-67

Agent Discovery Integrity and Freshness Verification

unassigned
Clients must validate the origin, integrity, endpoint binding and freshness of agent discovery metadata before relying on it, and deployments using registries must define which registry operators and update semantics are trusted.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-AI06GR-22
CT-68

Capability-to-Authority Non-Inference Rule

unassigned
A capability, skill, provider, identity or endpoint advertisement must not be treated as evidence of delegated authority, operator accountability, assurance level, entitlement, or current permission without a separately evaluated authorization or trust-policy decision.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-AI05GR-22
CT-69

End-to-End Delegation Context Propagation

unassigned
Multi-agent task chains must preserve and enforce the originating principal, delegated capability, purpose, resource scope, approval constraints, validity interval, revocation state and permitted delegation depth at each downstream hop.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-AI07GR-23
CT-70

Callback Destination Ownership and Egress Validation

unassigned
Before sending asynchronous callbacks or push notifications, a server must validate the callback destination against policy, prevent access to prohibited network ranges, and where risk warrants verify endpoint ownership or possession.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-AI08GR-24
CT-71

Callback Authenticity Freshness and Task Binding

unassigned
Asynchronous notifications must be authenticated, integrity-protected, bound to the intended receiver and task, freshness-checked, and replay-resistant before they can change workflow state or trigger downstream action.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-AI08GR-24

Secondary Credential Audience Purpose and Delegation Constraint

unassigned
Credentials obtained for an agent to access a downstream service must be constrained to the intended audience, resource, purpose, lifetime and delegation depth, and must not be forwarded or exchanged unless that transitivity is explicitly authorised.

unassigned

Witnessed VRC Exchange — First Contact Across a Trust Gap

Phase 3–4: Member Admission / Ceremony Protocol
Ahmed (D3) initiates a connecting VRC ceremony with Laila (D2) via a mutual non-member introduction. Neither party has prior relational history. Laila's terms require multiple interactions before VRC exchange; Ahmed's terms decline biometric attestation. They negotiate a staged two-session ceremony with no hard timeout. The VTA holds ceremony state as PENDING across sessions without firing ABANDONED. On completion the outcome record captures ceremony type, duration, and mutual obligations.

Witnessed VRC Renewal — Constitutor Witness as Dispute Evidence

VRC Renewal / Ceremony Protocol / Restore
Sophie (D5) counter-proposes a witnessed VRC renewal with Remi, requiring Laila (D2) as constitutor witness (not attestor). Remi accepts. The VWC encodes Laila's role as constitutor. Two months later, Sophie invokes Restore after a revocation complaint from Remi. The outcome record and VWC together demonstrate the relationship was in good standing at renewal, with the witness's social standing behind it. The Redress HX profile is invoked; Sophie's appeal is upheld.

Witnessed VRC Exchange — Sybil Laundering via Social Engineering of Witness

Identity Fraud / Sybil / Ceremony Protocol
Viktor (B1) uses Phantom (M2) to social-engineer Laila (D2) into witnessing a VRC exchange between two synthetic identities (Marco and Petra) by fabricating a plausible shared-event context. Laila's pre-ceremony terms require independent verification of both parties. She queries the registry: both show single-jurisdiction VRC graphs with anomalous timing. Laila invokes INDIRECT_DECLINE, committing her reason to the community governance log. The log entry triggers Tomasz's (D6) Sybil cluster investigation. The attack fails before any credential is issued; the failure record is created and referenced in subsequent anomaly detection.

Cross-VTC Credential Recognition — Ahmed Joins a Second VTC

Cross-VTC Interoperability
Ahmed holds a valid VRC from Laila's VTC and applies to join a second affiliated VTC. The second VTC's admission policy accepts one cross-VTC VRC as a substitute for one of its required two VRCs, provided the issuing VTC is on its trust registry. The receiving VTA must resolve the issuing VTC's C-DID, verify its governance framework version, retrieve the dependency map for Ahmed's VRC, and confirm no cascade revocation has occurred. If Ahmed's first-VTC membership is later revoked, the second VTC must be notified via the dependency map mechanism.

Governance Amendment — Daniel Updates the Constitution Mid-Lifecycle

Governance Amendment / Lifecycle
After a governance vote, Daniel amends the VTC admission threshold from two VRCs to three. Version 1.1 of the governance framework is published with a defined effective date. Ceremonies that reached AGREED state before the effective date are bound to version 1.0 and must complete under those rules. New ceremonies initiated after the effective date apply version 1.1. The VTA's PEP must enforce version binding at ceremony AGREED state. A member who was mid-ceremony at the effective date must not have their in-progress ceremony invalidated by the amendment.

Adjudication — Independent Review of a Disputed Anchor Denial

Adjudication / Appeals
Laila denies Ahmed's VRC application. Ahmed believes the denial is discriminatory and initiates a formal adjudication request. An independent governance body — not Laila, not Daniel, not any party to the original ceremony — is appointed as adjudicator. The adjudicator reviews the ceremony profile, the denial failure record, Ahmed's terms declaration, and Laila's registry query evidence. The adjudicator issues a binding ruling artefact. The VTA is required to honour the ruling. If the ruling overturns the denial, Laila must re-enter the ceremony or a substitute anchor must be appointed.

Agent Liveness Failure — Aether Continues Acting After Operator Revocation

Agent Liveness / Lifecycle
Aether (M1) is managing credential renewals for its operator. The operator's VMC is revoked for a governance violation. Aether has declared a behavioural commitment with a liveness check interval of five minutes. For up to five minutes, Aether continues to execute delegated exchanges on behalf of a revoked member. On the next liveness check, Aether detects the revocation, ceases all operations, and produces a signed suspension record referencing the operator's revocation timestamp and the list of actions taken during the harm window. The suspension record is submitted to the VTC governance log.

Behavioural Commitment Enforcement — Phantom Exceeds Its Declared Envelope

Behavioural Commitment Enforcement / Security
Phantom (M2) has registered with a legitimate operator credential and declared a behavioural commitment: maximum 10 credential presentations per hour, interactions limited to VTC members, no ceremony initiations. Phantom begins exceeding these parameters: 400 presentations per hour, ceremony initiations with non-members, parallel policy fuzzing. Each violation is compared against Phantom's signed behavioural commitment. The VTA generates breach records — cryptographically provable deviations from declared parameters — rather than relying solely on statistical anomaly detection. The breach records trigger a Restore task and Phantom's operator credential is suspended pending investigation.

Ecological Entity as First-Class Party — Sensor Network in a Land-Use Ceremony

Entangled Systems / Non-Human Entity
A river basin sensor network holds a DID granted by the relevant jurisdiction (analogous to the Whanganui River's legal personhood in New Zealand). A construction company proposes a land-use exchange with the river basin authority. Under the applicable governance framework, the sensor network is a named party in the Exchange — it declares terms (minimum flow rate thresholds must be maintained; no construction within 50m of the river bank), attests to current ecological state via a verifiable sensor credential, and can invoke Restore if the agreement is breached. The ceremony profile requires all five trust tasks to be executed with the sensor network as a named participant alongside the human parties.

Pre-Condition Violation — Exchange Initiated Without Prior Identify

Pre-condition Enforcement / Security
A developer integrating a VTC client application makes an implementation error: their code sends a ceremony PROPOSED message before completing DID resolution for the counterparty. The counterparty's M-DID is unresolved. The ceremony proceeds to PROPOSED state. At Level D, the signature check fails. The scenario tests whether the VTA's PEP enforces the Identify-before-Exchange pre-condition at the protocol layer (producing a standard pre-condition violation artefact) or whether the failure manifests as an implementation-specific runtime error with no interoperable representation.

Daniel's VTC is a community of open-source maintainers. Members endorse each other's contributions in specific domains (e.g., cryptography, governance design, accessibility). Laila endorses Ahmed for "decentralised identity protocol design" after collaborating on a proposal. Six months later, Laila retracts the endorsement — not because Ahmed did anything wrong, but because a later collaboration revealed a significant disagreement about approach. The retraction is prospective: it does not invalidate past decisions made on the basis of the endorsement, but Ahmed's current reputation profile no longer includes it. A recruiter queries the endorsement graph and the topology is verifiable for anomalous clustering.

VTC Dissolution — Winding Down with Full Member Portability

VTC Lifecycle / Dissolution
Daniel's VTC passes a governance vote to dissolve. The dissolution protocol requires: (1) all members notified within 24 hours via Signal; (2) all VMCs revoked via Lifecycle Transition; (3) the Community DID deactivated; (4) the tamper-evident governance ledger preserved and transferred to a designated archive; (5) each member issued a portability package containing their VMC (with dissolution record attached), all outcome records from ceremonies they participated in, all VWCs and endorsements, and the signed dissolution record; (6) a historical legitimacy binding — a signed assertion that all credentials issued before the dissolution date were valid at issuance — so other VTCs can verify the historical record.

Governance Configuration Failure — VTA Applies Wrong Framework Version to Live Ceremony

Governance Configuration / Security
A deployment error causes a VTA to apply governance framework version 1.1 (the amended three-VRC threshold) to a ceremony that was AGREED under version 1.0 (the two-VRC threshold). At Level B, the PEP rejects a sub-exchange that was valid under 1.0 but not under 1.1, producing an unexpected FAILED terminal state for a ceremony whose parties did nothing wrong. The failure record must capture the version mismatch in a machine-readable form. The parties invoke Restore. The Restore task must determine whether the failure was a protocol error (PEP applied wrong version), a governance error (version effective date was set incorrectly), or an implementation error (VTA deployment bug).

Organisational Identity & NHS Interoperability

Define how a regulated public sector organisation (NHS Foundation Trust) participates in the DTG as an organisational member: C-DID model adequacy, Caldicott Guardian as trust anchor with personal accountability, near-real-time revocation at staff-passport scale, cross-Trust credential interoperability, NHS data residency enforcement, and alignment with DCB3051 and NHS CIS2.

Recommendations

9 records
REC-1

Uniqueness Enforcement as Phase-Gate

proposednormative
GR-07 and CT-08 must become normative MUST requirements in the DTG credential specification. The VTC must define and document its uniqueness enforcement mechanism before Phase 4 opens. This is the single highest-coverage control requirement identified in this analysis, addressing Sybil proliferation, AI-mediated identity fraud, and the open issues cluster simultaneously. The specification should define at least three acceptable uniqueness mechanisms (ZKP personhood proof, trusted IDVP quorum, social recovery) and require governing bodies to select and document one.
Related RAHP artefacts
GR-07CT-08
REC-2

AI Agent Governance as First-Class Specification Area

proposednormative
All four AI Agent risks are rated High severity. The DTG credential specification must include a dedicated AI agent governance chapter covering: (a) cryptographic delegation scope constraints (CT-30) as a normative MUST; (b) operator VMC liveness checks before agent actions (CT-32) as a normative MUST; (c) non-human actor detection as a Phase 4 pre-condition (GR-14). This is a gap in all existing VC/DID standards — none address autonomous agent participation in trust graphs.
Related RAHP artefacts
GR-14CT-30CT-32
REC-3

Privacy-Preserving Revocation as Core Specification Requirement

proposednormative
GR-09 (Privacy-Preserving Revocation Disclosure) and CT-24 address 8 risks in total. The specification must require privacy-preserving revocation status mechanisms (e.g. W3C Status List 2021 with ZKP) as a normative MUST, not an optional feature. VTC-scoped revocation (CT-26) must also be normative: cross-VTC revocation contamination is a human rights risk that arises directly from the decentralised architecture.
Related RAHP artefacts
GR-09CT-24CT-26
REC-4

Non-Discriminatory Admission and Alternative Identity Proofing

proposednormative
RK-ID02 (Social Graph Privilege Exclusion) and RK-HX02 (Discriminatory Vouching) are both rated High severity and High likelihood — the most urgent combination in the dataset. The specification must require: (a) published non-discriminatory admission criteria; (b) at least one admission pathway not requiring conventional government-issued ID; (c) a documented appeals process for denied applicants. These are simultaneously legal requirements under equality and human rights law in most jurisdictions.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-HX02RK-ID02
REC-5

Multi-Party Registry Write Authorisation

proposednormative
CT-45 and GR-10 address trust graph capture, state coercion, and registry manipulation. Multi-party write authorisation must be a normative MUST in the DTG trust registry specification. The specification should define minimum threshold requirements (e.g. 2-of-3 for small VTCs, higher thresholds at scale) and require tamper-evident audit trails for all writes.
Related RAHP artefacts
GR-10CT-45
REC-6

Formal Threat Model as Standards Deliverable

proposedrecommended
GR-16 and CT-48 require a formal threat model. The DTGWG should publish this as a standalone deliverable alongside the credential specification. The threat model should be normatively referenced in the specification so that implementations can demonstrate conformance.
Related RAHP artefacts
GR-16CT-48
REC-7

UX Design Principles as Normative Standards Annex

proposedrecommended
RK-NM01 is rated High severity and High likelihood — and the DTGWG itself acknowledges UX as 'the single hardest problem'. Sovereign wallet UX design principles (CT-20) and non-technical user onboarding testing requirements (CT-21) should be published as a normative annex to the credential specification, not left to individual implementations. Poor UX creates security failures, not just usability problems.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-NM01CT-20CT-21
REC-8

Mandatory Open Issues Resolution Before Phase 4

proposedprocess
GR-17 requires the four bootstrapping open issues to be formally resolved or risk-accepted before Phase 4. The DTGWG standards process should define a formal phase-gate procedure: any VTC implementation claiming conformance to the DTG specification must demonstrate that each open issue has either a documented mitigation or a signed risk acceptance with a review date.
Related RAHP artefacts
GR-17
REC-9

Organisational Member Credential Type and Supported Decision-Making Credential Extensions

proposednormative
The DTG Credential Specification must define two new credential types as normative additions. First, the Organisational Member Credential (OMC): a credential type for legal entities (companies, public bodies, NHS Trusts, charities) participating as VTC members. The OMC must carry: the organisation's legal identifier (Companies House number, NHS ODS code, etc.); the DIDs of named responsible officers; a governance conformance attestation mapping the organisation's internal governance to the VTC governance conformance class; and data residency declarations. Without this, the DTG ecosystem cannot accommodate regulated institutions — a class that includes every NHS Trust, local authority, and regulated financial entity in the UK. Second, the Legal Delegation Credential (LDC): a scope-limited delegation credential representing a registered legal authority (Lasting Power of Attorney, court deputyship, or equivalent). The LDC must distinguish co-signed supported consent from substituted decision-making; name the attorney and donor DIDs; reference the legal instrument by registration number; and support a secondary notification recipient mechanism for governance communications. Both credential types address risks currently rated High or Critical (RK-EX04, RK-EX05, RK-HX04, RK-HX05, RK-SC05) and are required for compliance with the Mental Capacity Act 2005, UK Online Safety Act 2023, and NHS Digital Staff Passport programme requirements. These are specification-layer gaps — they cannot be resolved by controls or guardrails alone.
Related RAHP artefacts
RK-EX04RK-EX05RK-HX04RK-HX05RK-SC05

RA-001

Governanceless VTC claiming credential compliance

Cannot be fully mitigated without a normative governance conformance class in the DTG Credential Specification. CT-56 proposes one; it is not yet in the specification. Until the authority model is settled this is recorded as an open decision, not an acceptance.

RA-002

Sybil identity proliferation — uniqueness enforcement absent from spec v0.3

Scored High severity x High likelihood. GR-07 and CT-08 are the designated mitigations and are completely absent from DTG Credential Specification v0.3. Either the specification adopts REC-1 or the working group records a signed acceptance of an unmitigated 9-score risk. There is presently no process for the latter.

Open issues left unresolved at scale

GP-001

Bilateral VRC signatures accepted as partial GR-04 implementation

proposed
Full threshold signing imposes a UX burden incompatible with EPIC-12 (UX & Human Workflows) at current tooling maturity. Bilateral signing accepted as an interim measure, with GR-04 retained as a future normative candidate rather than closed.

GP-002

R-DID per-relationship requirement reduces linkability risk

proposed
A specification change that measurably reduces an assessed risk should be recorded as precedent, not merely reflected in a changed score. Without the record, a future revision could reverse the design choice without anyone noticing the risk score was contingent on it.

GP-003

M-DID bootstrapping exception permitted without a migration trigger

proposed
Recorded as a precedent because it is a decision the working group may not have taken deliberately. The exception is reasonable for bootstrapping; the absence of a migration trigger is what converts a temporary allowance into a permanent weakening of the R-DID privacy model. CT-50 and GR-18 propose the trigger.

DTG lifecycle & gaps

The portable RAHP lifecycle applied to the DTG deployment, with DTG-specific gaps shown as tracked records.

generated by tools/build.py from data/ · 48 risk · 73 control · 25 guardrail · 25 assurance_test · 40 metric · 36 user_story · 33 scenario · 21 epic · 22 persona · 9 recommendation · 3 risk_acceptance · 3 governance_precedent · 1 rule_profile · 5 evidence_artifact

Core principle. People and implementation context drive everything. Every risk score, control, guardrail, assurance test, trust metric and user story is only as analytically sound as the Context stage that preceded it. The toolkit is not a framework applied to a system — it is derived from a community.

STAGE-1 · Context & scoping

The generative engine. Community inquiry, extreme user and bad-actor identification, persona synthesis, and context validation.
Input artefacts
Working group charter, Problem statement, Technical scope, Threat intelligence
Produces
persona
Required outputs
Raw participant map; Implementation context document; Extreme user profiles; Bad-actor persona drafts; Validated context baseline and objectives map
Evidence required
Signed-off persona register with named contributor and source material per persona
GAP-1.1 — No defined standard for how much community inquiry is sufficient before Phase B can begin.
GAP-1.2 — No protocol for representing communities who cannot participate directly (children, people in high-risk political contexts, future users). The Verifiable AI SDJ methodology (Hickman, 2025) is a partial approach, not yet integrated into the workflow.

STAGE-2 · Drafting

Continuous risk-design-control loop. Every significant design choice is proposed, assessed, controlled and documented before acceptance into the draft.
Input artefacts
Validated persona set, Risk register, Draft specification text
Produces
risk, control, guardrail, assurance_test, metric, user_story, scenario
Required outputs
Risk-control mapping with rationale; Provenance-tagged toolkit additions
Evidence required
For each accepted design choice — the affected risks, the selected controls, the metric linkage, and the provenance tag naming the design decision and specification version that triggered it.
GAP-2.1 — No defined protocol for what constitutes adequate control coverage before a design choice is accepted into the draft.
GAP-2.2 — No agreed threshold for when a newly surfaced risk requires a full persona update versus a note in the register.

STAGE-3 · Review & harmonisation

Three parallel tracks — cross-standard alignment, community review, formal risk acceptance — converging at a harmonisation point before publication.
Input artefacts
Draft specification, Risk register, Adjacent standards
Produces
recommendation, risk_acceptance, spec_review
Required outputs
Specification gap analysis; Updated risk/control/guardrail/assurance records; REC records
Evidence required
Specification commentary report; every risk either adequately controlled or formally accepted with named authority and review date
GAP-3.1 — Formal risk acceptance workflow not yet defined — who can accept a risk, under what authority, for how long, with what documentation. The most significant process gap in the toolkit.
addressed by data/risk-acceptances.yaml (schema exists; authority model still undecided)
GAP-3.2 — No defined process for community outreach during review; passive invitation is insufficient.
GAP-3.3 — No protocol for translating community feedback not expressed in standards language into artefact updates.

STAGE-4 · Publication

Point-in-time event with ongoing implications. The toolkit snapshot is version-bound to the standard version and transitions from development tool to implementation support tool.
Input artefacts
Validated artefact set
Produces
conformance_claim
Required outputs
Normative candidate list; Assurance test suite; Tagged release; CHANGELOG entry
Evidence required
Conformance claim template; bidirectional version binding between toolkit version and specification version
GAP-4.1 — No implementation guidance document bridging toolkit artefacts and common deployment patterns.
GAP-4.2 — No structured intake process for collecting implementation experience from early adopters.

STAGE-5 · Maintenance

The longest and most underserved stage. Three trigger streams feed a triage and integration process on an annual review cadence, with continuous monitoring between reviews.
Input artefacts
Field reports, Threat model review, Specification revisions
Produces
risk, governance_precedent, changelog_entry
Required outputs
Updated records; New risks; Diff-annotated changelog entry
Evidence required
Dated review record covering all three trigger streams and the periodic extreme user review
GAP-5.1 — Contribution and integration governance not defined — no triage process, no acceptance authority, no decision on what enters the next toolkit version.
GAP-5.2 — No structured intake process for operational experience reports from implementors.
GAP-5.3 — No monitoring process specified for threat landscape tracking between annual reviews.
GAP-5.4 — Governance precedent records not yet in use — decisions are not retained between governance sessions.
addressed by data/governance-precedents.yaml
GAP-5.5 — Feedback loop design deliberately deferred pending practitioner trials. The loop must be empirically grounded, not designed in theory and imposed on practitioners.

Governance precedents

3 records
IDPrecedentLinkedStatus
GP-001
Bilateral VRC signatures accepted as partial GR-04 implementation
Full threshold signing imposes a UX burden incompatible with EPIC-12 (UX & Human Workflows) at current tooling maturity. Bilateral signing accepted as an interim measure, with GR-04 retained as a future normative candidate rather than closed.
 RK-ID01RK-ID03RK-AI03GR-04 proposed
GP-002
R-DID per-relationship requirement reduces linkability risk
A specification change that measurably reduces an assessed risk should be recorded as precedent, not merely reflected in a changed score. Without the record, a future revision could reverse the design choice without anyone noticing the risk score was contingent on it.
 RK-ID05 proposed
GP-003
M-DID bootstrapping exception permitted without a migration trigger
Recorded as a precedent because it is a decision the working group may not have taken deliberately. The exception is reasonable for bootstrapping; the absence of a migration trigger is what converts a temporary allowance into a permanent weakening of the R-DID privacy model. CT-50 and GR-18 propose
RK-SC04GR-18 proposed
